2561.sourceSearchName: stored program computer stored program computer
2561.title: Stored-Program Computer
2561.heading: Stored-Program Computer
2561.content:
A stored-program computer keeps machine instructions in the same internal memory system used for data. The processor can fetch its next instruction at electronic speed instead of waiting for an external card deck, tape, or patch board.

This organization made programs easier to load and change and enabled code generated as data to be executed. It became the basis of most commercial computers after the 1940s.

2562.title: Stored-Program Computer

2564.title: Stored Procedure
2564.heading: Stored Procedure
2564.content:
A stored procedure is a named database routine that can be invoked with parameters. A Dapper repository can specify the procedure name and command type, then map its returned rows in the same manner as an inline query.

Stored procedures place selected data behavior inside the database. The application still needs an explicit contract for parameter names, result columns, and how the procedure evolves with schema changes.

2567.title: Storage Redundancy
2567.heading: Storage Redundancy
2567.content:
Storage redundancy replicates cloud data across more than one failure boundary. Copies may be placed on separate machines, in separate facilities, or in another geographic area depending on the selected durability level.

Replication reduces the likelihood that one hardware or regional event destroys the only copy, but no service promises absolute safety. Greater separation and resilience generally increase cost, so the required failure tolerance must be chosen explicitly.

2569.title: Storage Communication Channel

2570.title: Storage Communication Channel
2570.heading: Storage Communication Channel
2570.content:
A storage communication channel is a logical connection that associates request queues, response handling, buffers, and endpoint state between a storage client and server. It gives concurrent operations an identifiable path through the protocol.

Multiple channels can separate flows and expose parallelism, but their state and ordering rules must remain coordinated with the underlying network interface.

2573.title: Stoichiometric Aviation Fuel Combustion
2573.heading: Stoichiometric Aviation Fuel Combustion
2573.content: Stoichiometric combustion supplies the theoretical minimum oxygen needed to oxidize a fuel completely. For an octane model of aviation gasoline, the ideal products are carbon dioxide, water, and nitrogen carried with the air. Too little oxygen promotes incomplete products such as carbon monoxide, while additional air changes temperature and composition as described in [[Excess Air and Adiabatic Flame Temperature]].

2576.title: Stop-Word Removal
2576.heading: Stop-Word Removal
2576.content:
Stop-word removal deletes very common function words that often contribute grammatical structure but little topic discrimination. Removing articles, determiners, and similar terms can shrink a vocabulary and reduce the number of text features.

The operation is task dependent. Function words may be uninformative for topical retrieval yet useful for authorship, style, or syntax analysis. A stop list should therefore reflect the representation's purpose rather than be applied automatically to every corpus.

2579.title: Stock
2579.heading: Stock
2579.content:
A stock is a container that accumulates and holds a [[Resource]]. Its state is the amount currently stored, and it may have a maximum capacity or be effectively unbounded.

Stocks make time visible in a system because inflows and outflows change their contents at particular rates. Bank balances, health pools, inventories, and populations can all function as stocks in a systemic model.

2582.sourceSearchName: stl mesh format stl mesh format
2582.title: STL Mesh Format
2582.heading: STL Mesh Format
2582.content:
STL represents a surface as triangular facets and is common in engineering, CAD, and fabrication workflows. It can be stored in text or binary form and records a normal and three vertices for each triangle.

The format does not use shared vertex indices and does not carry texture coordinates in the representation discussed by the source. Vertices are therefore repeated wherever triangles meet. That redundancy makes STL less compact than an indexed mesh, but its simple triangular structure gives it broad interchange value for geometric surfaces.

2584.title: STIRR Weight Propagation
2584.heading: Document

2585.sourceSearchName: stirr weight propagation stirr weight propagation
2585.title: STIRR Weight Propagation
2585.heading: STIRR Weight Propagation
2585.content:
STIRR weight propagation updates an attribute-value node from the weights of the other values appearing with it in database tuples. A combiner function aggregates each tuple's influence, after which the configuration is normalized.

Repeated reinforcement is transitive: values strongly related to an initial or emerging pattern pass influence through their shared records.

2586.sourceSearchName: stirr weight propagation stirr weight propagation
2586.title: STIRR Weight Propagation
2586.heading: References

2587.sourceSearchName: stirr fixed point stirr fixed point
2587.title: STIRR Fixed Point
2587.heading: Document

2588.sourceSearchName: stirr fixed point stirr fixed point
2588.title: STIRR Fixed Point
2588.heading: STIRR Fixed Point
2588.content:
A STIRR fixed point is a normalized weight configuration that no longer changes under the relational reinforcement function. At that point further propagation produces the same weights.

The positive and negative basins of the fixed configuration can separate groups of attribute values. Convergence depends on the combiner and starting conditions.

2589.sourceSearchName: stirr fixed point stirr fixed point
2589.title: STIRR Fixed Point
2589.heading: References

2591.title: STIRR Clustering
2591.heading: STIRR Clustering
2591.content:
STIRR, Sieving Through Iterated Relational Reinforcement, represents categorical attribute values as weighted graph or hypergraph nodes. Tuples connect the values that occur together.

An iterative nonlinear system propagates weights through those relations until a fixed point is reached. Values with related co-occurrence patterns develop compatible weights and can be isolated as groups.

2593.sourceSearchName: sting statistical information grid sting statistical information grid
2593.title: STING Statistical Information Grid
2593.heading: Document

2594.sourceSearchName: sting statistical information grid sting statistical information grid
2594.title: STING Statistical Information Grid
2594.heading: STING Statistical Information Grid
2594.content:
STING divides space into hierarchical cells and stores statistical summaries such as count, mean, variance, minimum, maximum, and distribution type for each cell. Queries and cluster decisions can then operate on summaries rather than raw points.

Higher-level cell statistics can be derived from children, enabling fast top-down pruning. The efficiency comes at the cost of axis-aligned boundaries and possible loss of fine structure inside summarized cells.

2595.sourceSearchName: sting statistical information grid sting statistical information grid
2595.title: STING Statistical Information Grid
2595.heading: References

2597.title: STIDF Object
2597.heading: STIDF Object
2597.content: An `STIDF` object stores attributes for an [[Irregular Space-Time Layout]] in which each observation has its own position and time. It does not assume repeated locations, shared sampling dates, or a complete space-time lattice. This flexibility suits opportunistic measurements but prevents direct array operations that rely on common indexes. Visualization often begins by grouping, interpolating, or otherwise organizing its observed pairs.

2599.sourceSearchName: stimulation preference in games stimulation preference in games
2599.title: Stimulation Preference in Games
2599.heading: Document

2600.sourceSearchName: stimulation preference in games stimulation preference in games
2600.title: Stimulation Preference in Games
2600.heading: Stimulation Preference in Games
2600.content:
Stimulation preference concerns the amount of social and sensory activity a player wants. The source associates it with extraversion: some players seek lively multiplayer interaction, while others prefer solitary play with fewer external demands.

The preference affects competition modes, communication features, pacing, and presentation. More stimulation is not automatically better when it overwhelms the audience the game intends to serve.

2601.sourceSearchName: stimulation preference in games stimulation preference in games
2601.title: Stimulation Preference in Games
2601.heading: References

2603.title: STFDF Object
2603.heading: STFDF Object
2603.content: An `STFDF` object stores attribute data for a [[Full Space-Time Grid]] defined by spatial features and a time index. With $n$ locations and $m$ times, its data frame follows an $n m$ row ordering in which the spatial index moves faster than the temporal index. A space-wide multivariate time series can be reshaped and vectorized into this order before constructing the object.

2606.sourceSearchName: sterile cockpit discipline sterile cockpit discipline
2606.title: Sterile Cockpit Discipline
2606.heading: Sterile Cockpit Discipline
2606.content: Sterile cockpit discipline excludes nonessential duties and conversation during critical phases of flight. Taxi, takeoff, landing, and non-cruise operations below the specified altitude demand attention to aircraft control, communication, and checklists. The rule converts lessons from distraction-related accidents into a shared boundary on crew activity.

2608.sourceSearchName: stereo window placement stereo window placement
2608.title: Stereo Window Placement
2608.heading: Document

2609.sourceSearchName: stereo window placement stereo window placement
2609.title: Stereo Window Placement
2609.heading: Stereo Window Placement
2609.content: Aligning the two eye images at a particular subject establishes the depth that seems to coincide with the physical screen, or stereo window. Aligning a distant subject makes nearer material appear in front of the screen; aligning a nearer subject makes more of the scene appear behind it. The book compares several alignments of three depth-staged models to show the difference. Dramatic foreground pop-out is a creative option, not a default; excessive separation can strain the viewing experience. See [[Stereo Parallax and Convergence]].

2610.sourceSearchName: stereo window placement stereo window placement
2610.title: Stereo Window Placement
2610.heading: References

2612.title: Stereolithographic Bioprinting
2612.heading: Stereolithographic Bioprinting
2612.content:
Stereolithographic bioprinting selectively exposes a photosensitive cell-compatible polymer to light, solidifying patterned regions one layer at a time. It can produce fine features and change cell or material composition between layers.

Photoinitiator toxicity, light exposure, material switching, resolution, and cell density constrain biological performance.

2614.sourceSearchName: stereo parallax and convergence stereo parallax and convergence
2614.title: Stereo Parallax and Convergence
2614.heading: Document

2615.sourceSearchName: stereo parallax and convergence stereo parallax and convergence
2615.title: Stereo Parallax and Convergence
2615.heading: Stereo Parallax and Convergence
2615.content: Because eyes occupy different positions, a nearby object appears to shift farther between left and right views than a distant one. This positional difference is stereo parallax. Convergence describes the location where the paired views are brought into alignment, influencing which depth appears to lie at the physical screen. The book's finger experiment makes the changing parallax visible by alternating eyes while moving a finger away. A stereo pair must preserve enough difference for depth without making its alignment uncomfortable. See [[Stereo Window Placement]].

2616.sourceSearchName: stereo parallax and convergence stereo parallax and convergence
2616.title: Stereo Parallax and Convergence
2616.heading: References

2618.title: Stereo Panning
2618.heading: Stereo Panning
2618.content:
Stereo panning distributes a sound between left and right output channels according to its direction relative to the listener. A source on one side contributes more strongly to the corresponding channel.

Panning supplies a directional cue even without a full surround system. It is combined with [[Distance Attenuation]] and other spatial effects rather than replacing them.

2621.title: Stepwise Selection
2621.heading: Stepwise Selection
2621.content:
Stepwise selection alternates between adding candidate covariates and reconsidering variables already in the model. A previously retained term may be removed when its contribution changes after other terms enter.

This flexibility distinguishes it from strict [[Forward Selection]]. It does not eliminate specification uncertainty or guarantee the true model, so the process should remain constrained by a prespecified variable set, scientific reasoning, and transparent iteration records.

2623.sourceSearchName: stefan boltzmann radiation law stefan boltzmann radiation law
2623.title: Stefan-Boltzmann Radiation Law
2623.heading: Document

2624.sourceSearchName: stefan boltzmann radiation law stefan boltzmann radiation law
2624.title: Stefan-Boltzmann Radiation Law
2624.heading: Stefan-Boltzmann Radiation Law
2624.content:
Any body above absolute zero emits thermal radiation. The net radiative heat rate between a surface and its surroundings is proportional to area, emissivity, the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, and the difference of their absolute temperatures raised to the fourth power.

The fourth-power dependence makes radiation increasingly important at high temperature and makes the governing equation nonlinear. Correct use requires Kelvin temperatures and credible [[Surface Emissivity and Absorptivity|surface optical properties]], not merely the temperature difference used in a convection relation.

2625.sourceSearchName: stefan boltzmann radiation law stefan boltzmann radiation law
2625.title: Stefan-Boltzmann Radiation Law
2625.heading: References

2626.sourceSearchName: steepest descent method steepest descent method
2626.title: Steepest Descent Method
2626.heading: Document

2627.sourceSearchName: steepest descent method steepest descent method
2627.title: Steepest Descent Method
2627.heading: Steepest Descent Method
2627.content:
The steepest descent method moves opposite the [[Gradient]], the direction of greatest first-order decrease of a differentiable objective.

Each iteration selects a step length along that direction and then recomputes the gradient. The method is conceptually simple but can progress slowly along narrow curved valleys.

2629.title: Steepest Ascent Method
2629.heading: Document

2630.sourceSearchName: steepest ascent method steepest ascent method
2630.title: Steepest Ascent Method
2630.heading: Steepest Ascent Method
2630.content:
The steepest ascent method iteratively moves in the direction of the [[Gradient]], which gives the greatest first-order increase of a differentiable objective.

A one-dimensional search chooses how far to move along that direction. Recomputing the gradient creates a new direction at each point, and the method stops when improvement or gradient magnitude is sufficiently small.

2633.title: Steam Power Plant
2633.heading: Steam Power Plant
2633.content: A steam power plant releases fuel heat in a boiler to raise high-pressure steam, expands that steam through a turbine, and drives an electrical generator. Its energy path passes from chemical to thermal to mechanical to electrical form. The source uses coal combustion as an example and notes that heat rejected in the condenser and stack limits overall conversion. See [[Combined-Cycle Power Plant]].

2636.sourceSearchName: steam methane reforming steam methane reforming
2636.title: Steam Methane Reforming
2636.heading: Steam Methane Reforming
2636.content: Steam methane reforming heats natural gas with steam to make a mixture including hydrogen and carbon monoxide. The source then converts much of the carbon monoxide with a [[Water-Gas Shift Reaction]] and removes carbon dioxide to obtain hydrogen-rich product gas. It is a fuel-processing route, so the hydrogen inherits energy and carbon consequences from the primary fossil feedstock.

2639.title: Steady and Transient Thermal Behavior
2639.heading: Steady and Transient Thermal Behavior
2639.content:
A thermal system is steady when its reported properties no longer vary with time. A transient model retains time as an independent variable and describes heating, cooling, storage, curing, or other evolution before equilibrium is reached.

A stationary answer can reveal the eventual operating condition but cannot reconstruct how the system got there. When peak temperature, warm-up time, or exposure history matters, [[Stationary and Time-Dependent Thermal Studies|time-dependent analysis]] is necessary even if a final steady state also exists.

2642.sourceSearchName: statistical software selection statistical software selection
2642.title: Statistical Software Selection
2642.heading: Statistical Software Selection
2642.content:
Statistical software selection matches an analytic environment to the data volume, existing code, team expertise, cost, support needs, output requirements, and organizational constraints of a project. No platform is universally superior across all of these dimensions.

R can offer accessible licensing, flexible graphics, and a broad package ecosystem, while SAS may be favored by legacy workflows, institutional support, very large datasets, or supplied SAS-format assets. The decision should be recorded as part of project design because it affects reproducibility and staffing.

2643.sourceSearchName: statistical software selection statistical software selection
2643.title: Statistical Software Selection
2643.heading: References

2644.sourceSearchName: statistical software licensing statistical software licensing
2644.title: Statistical Software Licensing
2644.heading: Document

2645.sourceSearchName: statistical software licensing statistical software licensing
2645.title: Statistical Software Licensing
2645.heading: Statistical Software Licensing
2645.content:
Statistical software licensing determines who may install, run, and distribute an analytic environment and which components are available. Proprietary systems may tie procedures, seats, renewal dates, or support to paid agreements, while open-source systems allow use without a license fee.

Licensing is part of analytic feasibility. A method that depends on an unavailable component cannot be reproduced by a collaborator, and a workflow affordable in a university may be impractical for a nonprofit or public-health organization outside that license.

2646.title: Statistical Software Licensing
2646.heading: References

2648.title: Statistical Power
2648.heading: Statistical Power
2648.content:
Statistical power is the probability that a study will reject a false null hypothesis under a specified effect, sample size, significance level, and analysis design. Higher power reduces the chance of missing an effect of the assumed magnitude.

Power is conditional rather than an intrinsic property of a dataset. Changing the test, outcome prevalence, allocation ratio, or anticipated [[Effect Size]] changes the sample size required to achieve a target such as 80 percent.

The source expresses power as the probability that a test statistic exceeds the chosen cutoff when the alternative is true. Its simulations show that increasing sample size narrows standard errors, separates the alternative distribution from the null, and increases the chance of detection.

2650.sourceSearchName: statistical language model statistical language model
2650.title: Statistical Language Model
2650.heading: Document

2651.sourceSearchName: statistical language model statistical language model
2651.title: Statistical Language Model
2651.heading: Statistical Language Model
2651.content:
A statistical language model assigns probabilities to word sequences. During speech recognition, it favors hypotheses that form plausible linguistic continuations even when the acoustic signal alone is ambiguous.

The language score is combined with the [[Acoustic Model]] during [[Speech Recognition Search]]. Traditional recognizers commonly use an [[N-Gram Language Model]], while neural systems can model longer context.

2652.sourceSearchName: statistical language model statistical language model
2652.title: Statistical Language Model
2652.heading: References

2653.sourceSearchName: statistical outlier detection statistical outlier detection
2653.title: Statistical Outlier Detection
2653.heading: Document

2654.sourceSearchName: statistical outlier detection statistical outlier detection
2654.title: Statistical Outlier Detection
2654.heading: Statistical Outlier Detection
2654.content:
Statistical outlier detection treats extreme observations as unlikely under an assumed or bounded distribution. Normal-theory rules, distribution-free inequalities, and covariance-aware distances provide candidate rejection regions.

The approach is vulnerable when outliers distort the estimated mean and spread. Robust estimators or iterative checking are needed when those parameters are not known independently.

2655.sourceSearchName: statistical outlier detection statistical outlier detection
2655.title: Statistical Outlier Detection
2655.heading: References

2657.title: Statistical Independence
2657.heading: Statistical Independence
2657.content:
Variables are statistically independent when their joint distribution factors into their marginal distributions: $P(X,Y)=P(X)P(Y)$. Learning one variable's value then does not change the distribution assigned to the other.

Independence is a strong claim and should not be substituted automatically for conditional independence. Two measurements can be dependent overall while becoming independent after the common state that influences both is known.

The source connects independence to causal structure and symmetry rather than treating it as a pattern justified only by observed frequencies. Determining whether factors operate independently requires considering the collective conditions that generate their outcomes.

2659.sourceSearchName: statistical function automation statistical function automation
2659.title: Statistical Function Automation
2659.heading: Document

2660.sourceSearchName: statistical function automation statistical function automation
2660.title: Statistical Function Automation
2660.heading: Statistical Function Automation
2660.content:
Statistical function automation packages a repeated analysis into a parameterized function or iteration. In R, a custom function names its inputs, performs the operations inside its body, and returns an object that can be reused across variables or datasets.

Loops and apply-family functions offer other ways to repeat work, such as creating the same contingency table for several covariates. Automation should follow a correct manual workflow: repeating an unclear or unvalidated operation only scales its mistakes.

2661.sourceSearchName: statistical function automation statistical function automation
2661.title: Statistical Function Automation
2661.heading: References

2662.sourceSearchName: statistical code module statistical code module
2662.title: Statistical Code Module
2662.heading: Document

2663.sourceSearchName: statistical code module statistical code module
2663.title: Statistical Code Module
2663.heading: Statistical Code Module
2663.content:
A statistical code module is a short file devoted to one coherent operation, such as importing data, checking distributions, recoding variables, fitting models, or producing tables. Focused modules make the purpose and output of each stage easier to inspect.

Modules should be organized into an explicit [[Reproducible Statistical Pipeline]]. When an early definition changes, the analyst can rerun the ordered stages and verify that every downstream dataset and result reflects the correction.

2664.sourceSearchName: statistical code module statistical code module
2664.title: Statistical Code Module
2664.heading: References

2666.title: Stationarity Feature
2666.heading: Stationarity Feature
2666.content:
A stationarity feature measures whether a time series maintains stable statistical behavior over time. Tests and summary statistics can indicate changes in level, variance, or other distributional properties.

Stationarity matters because many temporal models assume that their governing relationships do not drift. A feature encoding departures from that assumption can distinguish series and guide the choice of forecasting or transformation methods.

2669.title: Stationary and Time-Dependent Thermal Studies
2669.heading: Stationary and Time-Dependent Thermal Studies
2669.content:
A stationary study solves the state in which time derivatives vanish, making it appropriate for equilibrium operating conditions. A time-dependent study advances from an initial condition and records how temperature, flow, and stored energy evolve.

The choice follows the question rather than a preference for shorter runs. A stationary model cannot report warm-up time or transient overshoot, while a time-dependent model may use a stationary solution as an efficient initial state for later changing conditions.

2672.title: Stationary Point
2672.heading: Stationary Point
2672.content:
A stationary point of a differentiable function is a point where its [[Gradient]] is the zero vector. It is a candidate for an extremum, but it need not be a maximum or minimum.

The local classification depends on curvature. The [[Hessian Matrix]] can identify a [[Local Minimum]], [[Local Maximum]], or [[Saddle Point]] when its definiteness is conclusive.

2675.title: Stationarity Assumption
2675.heading: Stationarity Assumption
2675.content:
Training on historical records implicitly assumes that the learned relationships will remain useful when the model meets future cases. This is the stationarity assumption. It can fail when customers, incentives, policies, measurement systems, or other features of the domain change.

An evaluation on held-out historic data is therefore a necessary but incomplete check. A deployed model needs monitoring for changing inputs and outcomes so the organization can revisit its data, target, and model when the underlying process no longer resembles the past.

2678.title: Static, Dynamic, and Stagnation Pressure
2678.heading: Static, Dynamic, and Stagnation Pressure
2678.content: Static pressure is the local thermodynamic pressure of the air. Stagnation, or total, pressure is the pressure reached when a moving flow is brought to rest, and dynamic pressure is represented by the difference between total and static pressure. A pitot-static system uses that difference to infer [[Indicated, Calibrated, Equivalent, and True Airspeed]].

Once sliding starts, kinetic friction is usually lower, so the coefficient of static friction should not be substituted automatically for a moving interface.

2720.title: Standing Wave
2720.heading: Standing Wave
2720.content: A standing wave forms when similar waves traveling in opposite directions superpose. Fixed nodes have zero amplitude, while antinodes have maximum amplitude, and adjacent nodes are separated by half a wavelength. The pattern transfers no net energy along the medium and appears only at frequencies compatible with the boundary conditions.

2723.title: Standard Model
2723.heading: Standard Model
2723.content: The Standard Model organizes matter into quarks and leptons and describes electromagnetic, weak, and strong interactions through exchanged gauge bosons. The Higgs field accounts for particle masses within the theory. Gravity is not included, and observations such as dark matter show that the model is highly successful but not a complete account of nature.

2729.title: Standard Error
2729.heading: Standard Error
2729.content:
A standard error is the standard deviation of a statistic's [[Sampling Distribution]]. It measures how much the estimate would vary if the data-generating and sampling process were repeated.

For a sample mean under the [[Central Limit Theorem]], the population standard deviation is divided by the square root of sample size. In practice the unknown population spread is estimated, which introduces the t-distribution in small samples.

2732.heading: Standard Form of a Quadratic Equation
2732.content:
The standard form of a quadratic equation is

$$ax^2+bx+c=0,$$

with (a\neq0). Terms are collected on one side in descending powers, and the other side is zero.

Standard form exposes the coefficients used by the [[Quadratic Formula]] and permits factorization to use the [[Zero Product Property]]. An equation such as (8x^2-2x=15) becomes (8x^2-2x-15=0). Distributing, combining like terms, or clearing denominators may be required before the form is visible.

2738.title: Stakeholder Participation in AI Governance
2738.heading: Stakeholder Participation in AI Governance
2738.content:
Stakeholder participation in AI governance gives people affected by a system a role in defining its purpose, risks, rules, and evaluation. Relevant participants include developers and users as well as people who are classified, monitored, displaced, or exposed to consequences without choosing the system.

Participation supplies practical knowledge that expert-only policy can miss and gives democratic legitimacy to choices about shared futures. It is meaningful only when participants can change an outcome, not merely comment on a completed plan. Particular effort is needed to reach groups with less institutional power and those likely to carry the greatest risks.

2741.title: Stakeholder
2741.heading: Stakeholder
2741.content:
A stakeholder is a person or group with a meaningful interest in a product's outcome. Players, publishers, platform holders, business leaders, and dependent teams can each supply constraints, feedback, or value judgments.

Stakeholders collaborate through the [[Product Owner]] and inspect working results at the [[Sprint Review]]. Their participation grounds decisions in product evidence without turning the Development Team into a committee-controlled task pool.

2744.title: Staging Slot
2744.heading: Staging Slot
2744.content:
A staging slot is a nonproduction App Service destination used to host a release candidate before promotion. The deployment pipeline can install the new artifact there and run checks against an accessible environment.

Staging provides evidence about the deployable package and hosted configuration without immediately replacing production. It is useful only when its differences from production are understood and intentional.

2747.title: Staging Environment
2747.heading: Staging Environment
2747.content:
A staging environment is a pre-production deployment used to verify a published application under conditions closer to production than ordinary development. It creates a place to test configuration, hosting, networking, and deployment output before public release.

Staging should remain separate from production data and credentials while resembling the production topology closely enough to expose environment-specific faults.

2750.title: Staging Deployment
2750.heading: Staging Deployment
2750.content:
A staging deployment installs a release candidate into a nonproduction environment before live promotion. It provides a hosted destination for checking the artifact, environment settings, network relationships, and application startup.

Passing staging supplies additional release evidence but does not erase environmental differences. The pipeline must use the correct staging configuration and define how promotion follows verification.

2753.title: Stage Gate
2753.heading: Stage Gate
2753.content:
A stage gate is a deliberate checkpoint at which a project is evaluated for viability, progress, risk, and continued investment. A concept may pass forward, return for significant revision, or be removed from active development.

Stage gates bound an otherwise open-ended [[Design-Build-Test Loop]]. They allow exploration while preventing iteration from becoming indefinite motion without progress, and they preserve rejected ideas for possible future use rather than forcing sunk-cost continuation.

A gate can coexist with agile delivery when it evaluates demonstrated results, current risks, and updated forecasts. Treating the gate as approval of a frozen speculative plan instead suppresses the evidence that iteration was meant to produce.

2756.title: Stacked Generalization
2756.heading: Stacked Generalization
2756.content:
Stacked generalization trains a second-level model to combine predictions from several base classifiers. The combiner can learn that different models are reliable in different regions rather than using a fixed vote.

Its training inputs must be out-of-sample base predictions, commonly produced by cross-validation. Using predictions from models fitted on the same cases would leak training fit into the combiner and yield overoptimistic weights.

The first segment has a common baseline, while later segments do not, so subtle comparisons can be difficult. Frequencies, proportions, and the intended denominator should therefore be made explicit in the labels or accompanying table.

The book uses the stacked form to display a second category within each group and contrasts it with filled and dodged variants. That comparison makes the choice of denominator and baseline an explicit design decision.

2762.title: Stacked Autoencoder
2762.heading: Stacked Autoencoder
2762.content:
A stacked autoencoder builds a deep representation by placing several encoders in sequence. Layers may be pretrained one at a time as autoencoders before the entire stack is fine-tuned.

Successive hidden layers transform the input into increasingly abstract features. Bottlenecks, sparsity, denoising, and supervised objectives can be combined to shape the learned representation.

2786.content:
Squared error loss measures a prediction error by subtracting the desired output from the actual output and squaring the difference. Squaring removes the sign and penalizes larger differences more strongly.

For a predicted value of 0.2 and target of 1.0, the loss is $(0.2-1.0)^2=0.64$. It is a simple [[Loss Function]] for scalar outputs; classification across multiple probabilities may instead use [[Categorical Cross-Entropy]].

2789.title: Square
2789.heading: Square
2789.content:
The square of a quantity is its second power:

$$a^2=a\cdot a.$$

The name reflects the area of a geometric square with side length (a). Squaring a real number produces a nonnegative result, so ((-a)^2=a^2). Parentheses distinguish the square of a negative value from the opposite of a square. A quantity that equals the square of another number is a perfect square, and reversing the operation uses a [[Square Root]].

2792.heading: Square Root
2792.content:
A square root of (a) is a number whose [[Square]] equals (a). The radical notation (sqrt{a}) denotes the nonnegative square root when (a\geq0); for example, (sqrt{25}=5) because (5^2=25).

A positive number also has a negative value whose square is the same, which is why solving (x^2=25) gives (x=5) or (x=-5). If a natural number is not a perfect square, its square root is irrational. Negative real numbers do not have real square roots.

2795.title: Square of a Sum Identity
2795.heading: Square of a Sum Identity
2795.content:
The square of a sum identity is

$$(a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2.$$

It follows by distributing ((a+b)(a+b)). Geometrically, a square of side (a+b) divides into squares of areas (a^2) and (b^2) plus two rectangles of area (ab).

The middle term is essential: exponentiation does not distribute over addition. The identity can expand a squared binomial, recognize a perfect-square trinomial, or support mental arithmetic by choosing a nearby convenient value.

2798.title: Square of a Difference Identity
2798.heading: Square of a Difference Identity
2798.content:
The square of a difference identity is

$$(a-b)^2=a^2-2ab+b^2.$$

It follows from the [[Square of a Sum Identity]] by substituting (-b) for (b), or by directly distributing ((a-b)(a-b)). The first and last terms are positive squares, while the cross terms combine to (-2ab).

The identity is reversible: a trinomial with this exact structure factors as ((a-b)^2). It should not be confused with the [[Difference of Squares Identity]], which has no middle term.

2801.title: Square Matrix
2801.heading: Square Matrix
2801.content:
A square matrix has the same number of rows and columns, so its size is $n\times n$. Square shape permits operations and properties that rectangular matrices do not have, including a [[Determinant]], [[Matrix Trace]], eigenvalues, and possibly a [[Matrix Inverse]].

Important square-matrix families include [[Diagonal Matrix]], [[Upper Triangular Matrix]], [[Symmetric Matrix]], and [[Orthogonal Matrix]].

2804.title: SQLite Mobile Cache
2804.heading: SQLite Mobile Cache
2804.content:
A SQLite mobile cache stores structured application data in an embedded relational database on the device. It supports indexed queries and relationships that would be cumbersome in an unstructured key-value cache, while remaining available without a network connection.

Libraries such as SQLite.NET map .NET model attributes to tables and indexes. Local persistence does not itself synchronize with the server; the application must define which records are authoritative and how concurrent changes are resolved.

2807.title: SQL-on-Hadoop
2807.heading: SQL-on-Hadoop
2807.content:
SQL-on-Hadoop systems expose relational queries over data stored in the Hadoop ecosystem. They translate SQL into distributed operations while attempting to preserve familiar schemas, joins, aggregations, and business-intelligence access.

Systems differ in whether they use MapReduce, a long-running query engine, or Spark; whether they rely on Hive metadata; and how they trade interactive latency against fault tolerance and throughput.

2810.title: SQL Injection
2810.heading: SQL Injection
2810.content:
SQL injection occurs when untrusted input is interpreted as part of a database command rather than as a value. A flexible sorting or filtering endpoint can create this vulnerability if it inserts unchecked client expressions into a query.

The application should constrain selectable property names to known model fields and use parameterized values. Hiding the input in an Angular interface is insufficient because a client can construct its own [[HTTP Request]].

2813.title: Spyware
2813.heading: Spyware
2813.content:
Spyware secretly observes a user or system and collects information for another party. It may record activity, credentials, communications, browsing behavior, or device details, undermining [[Cybersecurity Confidentiality]] without immediately disrupting normal operation.

Because stealth is central to its value, spyware may prioritize persistence and quiet data transfer. Endpoint monitoring, least privilege, application control, and [[Extrusion Detection]] help reveal collection and unauthorized outbound movement.

2816.title: Spurious Correlation
2816.heading: Spurious Correlation
2816.content:
A spurious correlation is a statistical association that does not reflect the causal relationship a decision maker assumes. Variables may move together by chance, because both depend on another factor, or because the data collection process created the pattern.

Machine learning can exploit such associations successfully within training data while failing when conditions change. The ethical risk grows when correlation is used to judge a person, allocate an opportunity, or justify intervention. High predictive performance does not by itself establish that the inferred relationship is meaningful, fair, or appropriate for action.
